summary: Question: how to model and forecast yield curves for cash (LIBOR/Eurodollar) and commodity futures (crude, heating oil, natural gas, soybean) in one framework. Method: decompose the curve into unconditional, maturity-specific and date-specific mean-reverting components, fitted to contract-level data cleaned of microstructure anomalies. Conclusion (slides only, detail in a separate paper): out-of-sample forecasts beat a random walk in most commodity/horizon cells, but no trading strategy or P&L is presented.

coverage.note: definition of yield curve with 7 Nov 2008 treasury example
follow contracts rather than fixed maturity

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Curve on a given day is formed by connecting the rates over different maturities.
claims.claim: The yield curve on a date is the set of rates across maturities; the slide gives the 7 Nov 2008 Treasury curve as the example.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Interest rate on a 3-month contract in the future
claims.claim: The cash curve used in the paper is built from Eurodollar contracts (LIBOR): each contract gives the rate on a 3-month deposit starting at a future date, plotted as instantaneous forward rates.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Plot shows instantaneous forward rates.
claims.claim: The chart for 2008.16 (about Feb 2008) shows a forward curve that starts near 3.0-3.1% at the shortest maturities, dips to roughly 2% near tau 0.7-1, then rises to about 5.8% at tau 10 (read from chart, approximate).
claims.reported_result: 2008.16: forward rate ~3.1% at tau~0.25, trough ~2% near tau~0.7, ~4.0% at tau 4, ~5.8% at tau 10 (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Interest rates implied by the prices of contracts for delivery of a commodity at some future date.
claims.claim: A commodity 'yield' is the interest rate implied by futures prices at successive delivery dates, so each commodity has its own curve of the same form as the cash curve.
claims.indicator: Commodity futures-implied yield by delivery date

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Light crude oil, same date as prior slide
claims.claim: For light crude on the same date (2008.16) the implied yield is about -0.03 at the shortest maturities, crosses zero near tau 2.5 and reaches about +0.01 at tau 8-9 (read from chart, units labelled %, as printed).
claims.reported_result: Light crude 2008.16: ~-0.03 at tau<1, 0 near tau 2.5, ~+0.01 at tau 8.5 (approximate chart reading, axis labelled '%' as printed; the scale looks like a fraction)
claims.conditions: negative short-end yield means front prices above deferred prices (backwardation)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: How is the yield for cash related to yields implied by commodities that include convenience factors?
claims.claim: The authors pose, without answering on the slide, the link between the cash yield and commodity-implied yields, which contain a convenience-yield component.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Can you predict where it’s headed?
claims.claim: Stated aim: describe how fast the yield curve changes and whether its future shape can be predicted.
claims.testable: no - a question, not a finding

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Some changes are large, other curves cluster together
claims.claim: Over about 100 trading days the cash yield curve changes shape a lot at some points and little at others; the short end moves most (trough rises from about 3.0% to about 4.5%) while the long end (tau 6-10) stays near 5.5-6.0%.
claims.reported_result: Cash curves 10 trading days apart over ~100 days: short-end trough rises from ~3% (red, original) to ~4.5% (lightest grey); 10-year end stays ~5.6-6.1% (approximate chart reading)
claims.conditions: large short-end moves, small long-end moves

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Rather different appearance from cash, with much less smoothness
claims.claim: Light crude yield curves over the same 100 days are much rougher than cash curves and swing from about -0.10 to above zero at the short end.
claims.reported_result: Crude curves 10 trading days apart: short-end yields range from about -0.10 to -0.02 (approximate chart reading); long end converges near 0 to +0.01

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Strong seasonal pattern for heating oil that is not apparent in yield on light crude.
claims.claim: Heating oil yield movements over 10-day intervals show a strong seasonal cycle across contract maturity (swing of roughly +0.2 to -0.2 within one year of maturity) that light crude does not show.
claims.reported_result: HO 10-day yield changes peak near +0.2 at tau~0.4-0.7, trough near -0.2 at tau~0.9-1.0; CL changes stay within about -0.15 to +0.03 (approximate chart reading)
claims.indicator: 10-day changes in implied yield, heating oil (HO) vs light crude (CL), by maturity tau 0-1.4 years
claims.conditions: heating oil only; crude shows no comparable seasonality
claims.testable: partly - needs the raw futures data

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Rather than have to predict a “curve”, forecast the value of certain parameters in a regression- like formula for the curve
claims.claim: A parsimonious parametric model reduces curve forecasting to forecasting a few parameters of a polynomial-like formula.
claims.exact_rule: Express the whole curve as a low-dimensional parametric function and forecast its parameters rather than each maturity
claims.testable: yes - model form given in the paper

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Model used resembles a polynomial, but on a logarithmic scale more suited to description of rates.
claims.claim: The curve is modelled as a polynomial-type expansion on a logarithmic (exponential-decay) scale, which suits interest-rate shapes.
claims.exact_rule: Basis functions of the form exp(-k*tau)-type terms (see following slides) rather than ordinary polynomials in tau
claims.testable: partly - basis detail on the next slides, k not given

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Does the model allow arbitrage?
claims.claim: Two modelling issues left to the paper: how many polynomial terms to use, and whether the fitted model permits arbitrage.
claims.testable: no - open issues, not resolved on the slides

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Decompose the yield curve y t (τ) into three components
claims.claim: The yield curve at date t and maturity tau is split into an unconditional curve U(tau), a maturity-specific part M_t(tau) and a date-specific part D_t(tau).
claims.data_needed: Yield curve panel by date and maturity

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Long-term unconditional expectation
claims.claim: U(tau) is the long-run unconditional mean curve: the conditional expectation of the curve at any date equals U(tau) in the long run.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Maturity specific component is mean reverting
claims.claim: The maturity-specific component factors as m_t*g(tau), where m_t is log-normal and decays toward zero at rate k, so deviations tied to a given maturity mean-revert.
claims.exact_rule: M_t(tau)=m_t*g(tau); m_t log-normal SDE; E_s[m_t]=m_s*exp(-k(t-s)) for s<t
claims.testable: yes - SDE form given, k and g not specified on slides

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Date specific term is also mean reverting, but captures effects that move toward origin with time
claims.claim: The date-specific component D_t(tau) is attached to a contract's expiry date, so it slides toward tau=0 as time passes (E_s D_t(tau)=D_s(tau+t-s)) while also decaying, i.e. each contract carries its own date effect.
claims.exact_rule: E_s[D_t(tau)] = D_s(tau+t-s); if d_t is log-normal then h(tau)=exp(-k*tau) and E_s[D_t(tau)] = d_s*exp(-k(t-s))*exp(-k*tau)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Example (2,2,3)
claims.claim: The worked specification (2,2,3) has a second-order unconditional curve, two maturity-specific functions m1=c1*(e^{-k tau}-e^{-2k tau}) and m2=c2*(e^{-k tau}-e^{-4k tau}), and three date-specific functions.
claims.exact_rule: Orders (unconditional=2, maturity-specific=2, date-specific=3); maturity functions exp(-k tau)-exp(-2k tau) and exp(-k tau)-exp(-4k tau); constants c_m1, c_m2; k common shape constant
claims.testable: partly - k and c values not on slides

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Constant k determines shapes
claims.claim: Both the maturity-specific basis M_t(tau) (hump shape, peaking about 0.3 near tau 0.5) and the date-specific basis D_t(tau) (decaying from 1.0 at tau 0 toward 0 by tau 3) are controlled by a single constant k.
claims.reported_result: M_t(tau) peak about 0.3 near tau~0.5 and decays to ~0.1 by tau 3; D_t(tau) falls from 1.0 to ~0.1 by tau 3 (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Estimates are smoother than those for each day
claims.claim: The model's fitted state coefficients give a smoother curve than the raw day-by-day estimate; on 2006.87 the fitted curve (thick black) lies below the date-specific term and tracks the observed dots, with the date component dominating at the short end and the maturity component negative (to about -0.19).
claims.reported_result: 2006.87 fit: observed short-end value ~0.5 at tau 0 falling to ~0 by tau 2; maturity component dips to about -0.19 near tau 0.25; unconditional component about -0.07 at tau 0 (approximate chart reading)
claims.testable: partly - single date shown, no fit statistic

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Observation error ought to be uncorrelated
claims.claim: The fit is considered adequate only if observation errors are uncorrelated; the slide flags this as a diagnostic still to be checked.
claims.exact_rule: Check that residual (observation) errors from the fitted state model are serially/cross-sectionally uncorrelated

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Extrapolate fit
claims.claim: Forecasting method: take the fitted state, extrapolate it forward, and update it recursively as the forecast extends beyond the initial training period.
claims.exact_rule: Fit model on initial training window; extrapolate state forward; recursively re-fit/update as horizon extends past the training period; compare with a random-walk forecast
claims.testable: partly - training length, loss function and what is forecast (yield or price) not stated

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Negative values indicate our models dominate random walk (Newey-West statistic)
claims.claim: The table reports a Newey-West test statistic of the model against a random-walk benchmark; negative values mean the model forecasts better. Crude at 65 days is the only positive cell (2.1, random walk better); all other cells are negative.
claims.reported_result: Newey-West statistic (negative = model beats random walk). 65d/125d/250d: Crude 2.1/-0.09/-2.2; Heating Oil -5.8/-8.7/-2.2; Natural Gas -1.6/-2.2/-1.4; Soybean -5.1/-7.4/-3.1. (Exhibit slide 17; sample period, loss function and significance cut-off not stated)
claims.indicator: Newey-West statistic, model vs random walk forecast error
claims.conditions: fails for crude at 65 days; weakest evidence for crude (-0.09 at 125 days is insignificant)
claims.testable: partly - needs paper for sample and loss function

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Recursively update as forecast extends beyond initial training period
claims.claim: Horizons of 65, 125 and 250 days are the out-of-sample forecast horizons tested; the model's edge is strongest at 65-125 days for heating oil and soybean and shrinks at 250 days.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Obtain prices of futures contracts from data vendor CRB Trader
claims.claim: Raw inputs are futures contract prices from CRB Trader; yields are not observed directly and are derived from the prices.
claims.data_needed: Futures contract prices from CRB Trader (daily, by contract)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Prices are much smoother
claims.claim: The price curve across contracts is much smoother than the derived yield curve, so prices are the better object to inspect and clean.
claims.reported_result: 2008.16 light crude: price curve ~88-91 across tau 0-8, smooth; yields from the same data are jagged (about +-0.03)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Compute the yield at the midpoint between two observed prices as the continuously compounded rate of interest
claims.claim: Yield between adjacent contract maturities is the continuously compounded forward rate: y_t(tau) = [log p_t(tau+d) - log p_t(tau)]/d, evaluated at the midpoint of the two contracts.
claims.exact_rule: y_t(tau) = (log p_t(tau+d) - log p_t(tau)) / d, d = gap between adjacent contract expiries, assigned to the midpoint tau + d/2
claims.data_needed: Futures prices for adjacent contracts, expiry dates

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Differencing magnifies random noise
claims.claim: Taking log differences between neighbouring prices magnifies noise, and the curve is only observed at discrete maturities, the last contract being about 15 days out, with no observed spot rate.
claims.conditions: noise magnification worst for adjacent short-dated contracts; shortest contract about 15 days; no spot price observed

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Anomalies (aka, “market microstructure”)
claims.claim: Derived yields contain anomalies from market microstructure that have to be cleaned before modelling.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Ripple induced by preference for contract at a specific date (market microstructure)
claims.claim: Cash (LIBOR) curves show ripples at about 10-day spacing caused by traders' preference for contracts at specific dates, which is microstructure, not information about rates.
claims.reported_result: 1995.28 LIBOR curves: ripples visible in the 4-10 year range in three curves about 10 days apart (approximate chart reading)
claims.conditions: date-specific preference for particular contract expiries

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: A contract for light crude did not trade this day, so price stayed same as on prior day
claims.claim: A stale price (contract did not trade, previous close carried) distorts the derived yield curve and shifts the rest of the curve; the slide shows 1999.35.
claims.reported_result: 1999.35 light crude: yield spike to about +0.05 and -0.10 near tau 1-6; price curve ~16.0-17.2 with a flat segment (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Approach is to follow a contract over time rather than fixed maturity
claims.claim: Data cleaning is done by tracking each contract (fixed expiry date) through time instead of holding maturity tau fixed, which avoids interpolation-induced jumps; in the (t,tau) grid a contract is a diagonal where t+tau is constant.
claims.exact_rule: Index series by expiry date e = t + tau; clean each contract yield series along the diagonal rather than across maturities on a given day

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Contracts have a more consistent sequential pattern than in yields over varying maturities
claims.claim: Contracts show a more consistent sequential pattern over time than yields across maturities on a fixed date, so outliers are easier to detect along a contract.
claims.testable: yes - empirical claim shown in slide 24

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Outliers are more easily identified in the sequence of yields associated with contract rather than over the yield curve itself.
claims.claim: Spikes in the yield series of a single contract (a few points deviating from the smooth path, e.g. near day 35 550 at about 0.27) stand out and can be filtered, whereas on the curve it is unclear which wiggles are real.
claims.exact_rule: Detect outliers in each contract yield time series (see slide 25-26: moving median of length 3)
claims.reported_result: Single contract yield series days 35 200-35 900: path rises from ~0 to peak ~0.3 near day 35 750 then falls to about -0.2; isolated outliers (~0.27 near 35 550, -0.16 near 35 100) (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: In order not to distort “real” prices, miss a few outliers.
claims.claim: The cleaning filter is deliberately conservative: it accepts that a few outliers survive so that real price moves are not smoothed away.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Moving medians of length 3 cannot patch a period with a sustained anomaly.
claims.claim: The length-3 moving median repairs isolated outliers but not a sustained anomaly: one contract shows a break lasting about 3 weeks (yield falling to about -1.5 around days 35 650-35 700) that the filter cannot fix.
claims.exact_rule: Outlier patch = moving median of length 3 along the contract series
claims.reported_result: Anomaly persists about 3 weeks; yield dips to about -1.5 (approximate chart reading)
claims.conditions: fails for anomalies longer than about 2 observations

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Cannot hold maturity τ fixed unless were able to observe y t (τ) for all t
claims.claim: Time-series methods need a series at constant maturity, but yields at fixed tau are not observed on every day; interpolation to get them introduces artifacts.
claims.conditions: interpolation between observed contract points creates artifacts

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Following a single contract provides most direct series
claims.claim: Therefore the authors use the single-contract series as the primary time series, and keep the structural model f(tau) for evaluating the curve at any maturity and deriving quantities.
claims.exact_rule: Use contract-level yield series y_t(tau) with fixed expiry as the time series; structural model supplies f(tau) at any maturity

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Contracts end, becoming more variable as τ approaches 0 where yield is more volatile.
claims.claim: A contract's yield becomes more volatile as expiry approaches (tau to 0); the plotted contract (day 35694) swings between about -0.1 and 0.4 near its end.
claims.reported_result: Contract expiring day 35694: yield ~0 for first ~300 rows from expiration rising to a range of about -0.1 to +0.4 in the last ~100 rows (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Very strong presence of outliers as τ nears 0
claims.claim: Cross-contract standard deviation of yields rises sharply as expiry nears and the variation is non-Gaussian near the origin; the classical SD reaches about 0.33 at 0-10 rows to expiration, while a robust SD is only about 0.21.
claims.reported_result: SD vs rows to expiration: classical SD ~0.33 at 0, ~0.17 at 50, ~0.08 at 200, ~0.04 at 400; robust SD ~0.21 at 0, ~0.04 at 400 (approximate chart reading)
claims.conditions: heavy-tailed near expiry; use robust scale there

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Differences in yields of adjacent contracts are non-stationary as time gap increases
claims.claim: Differences between yields of adjacent contracts become non-stationary as the gap between their expiries widens, so contracts are cointegrated only when they are not too far apart.
claims.conditions: cointegration holds for nearby expiries only

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Interpret the source of non-stationarity as due to movements of some underlying yield process
claims.claim: The non-stationarity is attributed to a latent underlying yield process, motivating a latent-variable state model; the degree of time separation also measures how fast the curve changes (a stochastic modulus of continuity).
claims.exact_rule: Treat the curve as driven by a latent yield state; measure speed of curve change by the time gap at which adjacent-contract yield differences become non-stationary

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Prices again seem simpler to use
claims.claim: Light crude contract prices of four contracts about 100 days apart in mid-1984 move together in a smooth, parallel way, supporting the use of prices over yields.
claims.reported_result: Mid-1984, four light crude contracts: prices roughly 26-31 over about 500 days, nearly parallel (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Prices again seem simpler to use
claims.claim: In early 2007, four light crude contracts about 100 days apart again move together smoothly, with prices from about 55 to about 120 over the plotted span.
claims.reported_result: Early 2007, four light crude contracts: prices rise from about 55-60 to about 100-120 (approximate chart reading)

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Model after subtracting out the yield for cash to extract a convenience yield
claims.claim: Planned extension: subtract the cash yield from each commodity yield to isolate the convenience yield, which may be easier to model (possibly stationary).
claims.exact_rule: convenience yield_t(tau) = commodity-implied yield_t(tau) - cash yield_t(tau)
claims.data_needed: Commodity futures yields and LIBOR/Eurodollar cash yield

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: How to use the evident contemporaneous movements in prices or yields for various products (such as the various soy commodities)
claims.claim: Open problem: how to exploit the contemporaneous co-movement of yields across related products (e.g. soybean, soy meal, soy oil) in a multivariate model.

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Out-of-sample performance superior to random walk benchmark
claims.claim: The authors summarise that the model beats a random-walk benchmark out of sample (supported by the slide 17 Newey-West statistics, with crude at 65 days the exception).
claims.reported_result: See slide 17 table: 11 of 12 cells negative (model better); crude 65d +2.1
claims.testable: partly - sample details are in the paper

claims.speaker: Stine, Chua, Ramaswamy
claims.quote: Many unresolved questions
claims.claim: The slides present a work in progress with many unresolved questions and no trading application, transaction costs or portfolio results.
